questions.question: A patient presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness and a significantly elevated creatine kinase (CK) level following the initiation of a new medication. How does the clinical course of immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM) typically differ from that of direct drug-induced toxic rhabdomyolysis?

In the evaluation of a patient with suspected inflammatory myopathy, the myositis panel is negative for anti-HMGCR and anti-SRP antibodies. Does this exclude a diagnosis of immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM), and what is the estimated prevalence of seronegative IMNM?

On muscle biopsy, what are the characteristic histological hallmarks of immune-mediated necrotising myopathy (IMNM) that distinguish it from other inflammatory myopathies like polymyositis or dermatomyositis?

This patient presented with progressive proximal muscle weakness accompanied by dysphagia and dysphonia. What is the clinical significance of these bulbar symptoms in the context of an inflammatory myopathy, and what are the primary risks associated with them?

When evaluating a patient with severe muscle breakdown and elevated CK, why is it critical to cautiously interpret elevations in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT), and how can a clinician differentiate between hepatic and myogenic origins of these enzymes?

The patient in this case responded rapidly to a short course of high-dose corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) and was able to be weaned off immunosuppression quickly. How does this response pattern help differentiate a drug-triggered autoimmune process from an idiopathic autoimmune myopathy?
